title: Chitrakoot
hook: Rama walks Sita around the mountain and tells her he doesn't miss the kingdom at all
tomorrow: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chitrakoot as it is today, a pilgrim town where people walk barefoot around the hill. Did you feel the ground under your feet? Today, the last look at the exiles' happy days on the mountain. Day five hundred forty-one.

Every hard story has a pause somewhere, a stretch where the characters get to simply live. On Chitrakuta, the exiles get theirs. The hut is built. The days fall into a rhythm: bathing in the river, gathering fruit, sitting by the fire at night. And one day Rama takes Sita by the hand and walks her around the mountain, pointing things out, the way you'd show someone the neighborhood you've just moved into and already love.
screen: `EVERY HARD STORY HAS A PAUSE.` → `A RHYTHM TO THE DAYS.` → `SHOWING HER THE NEIGHBORHOOD.`

segments.voice: Look at the peaks, Rama tells Sita: some silver, some red, some yellow like gold, some the color of crystal. Look at the waterfalls, the flowering trees, the birds. Then he says something tender and surprising. Seeing this mountain with you, I don't grieve for the kingdom, and I don't miss my friends. Living here, he says, brings him two good things: he keeps his father's word, and he gives his brother Bharata joy. He takes her down to the Mandakini river. Its water is clear. Sages are bathing in it, raising their arms to the sun. Deer come down to drink. Bathe here with me, Rama says. And he says, in effect: think of this mountain as Ayodhya, think of the deer as the people of the city, and think of the Mandakini as our own river Sarayu. You may hear an echo from a few days back. Sumitra told Lakshmana: think of the forest as Ayodhya. Now Rama tells Sita the same thing, and on the mountain, it's true. A small honest note about the text. Valmiki actually tells this scene a little later, while trouble is already on its way to the mountain, and the contrast is part of his art. We've placed it here, at the end of the exiles' first days, because it's the clearest picture of what those days were like. Now we go back to where Valmiki's story actually runs next. Far away in Ayodhya, the charioteer Sumantra is driving home, alone, with an empty chariot. And an old king is waiting.
screen: `SILVER, RED AND GOLDEN PEAKS.` · `I DON'T GRIEVE FOR THE KINGDOM.` · `THE MANDAKINI IS OUR SARAYU.` · `THE CAMERA TURNS TO AYODHYA.` · then, large: `AN EMPTY CHARIOT GOES HOME.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Pick one small place in your life where things are good right now, a corner, a routine, a person you're with. Settle into it in your mind, the way the exiles settled on the mountain. On each breath in, notice one good detail about it. On each breath out, let it be enough, just as it is, for now. The bell holds the time.
Chitrakoot, the happy pause. Rama shows Sita the mountain and the Mandakini and tells her he doesn't miss the kingdom: this mountain is their Ayodhya now.
Your line: a hut on the hill. Today, find one small place to settle, and let it be your Ayodhya for an hour. Day five hundred forty-one.

screen: `DAY 541 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DASHARATHA'S DEATH AND THE CURSE.`

fork.setup: you're Rama, a prince living in a leaf hut on a mountain. Sita is beside you. what do you tell her?
options: we'll get the kingdom back someday.
I don't miss the kingdom; this mountain is our Ayodhya.

fork.reveal: Rama tells her the mountain with her is enough: he keeps his father's word, gives Bharata joy, and doesn't grieve for the kingdom.

original.note: Sanskrit mandākinī: the river at Chitrakuta where Rama and Sita bathe; still the river of Chitrakoot town.

trapdoor: what you thought: the exile was misery from start to finish.
what it means: at Chitrakuta, Rama tells Sita he doesn't miss the kingdom at all.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki sets Rama's description of the mountain and the river just before Bharata's army arrives, so the happiest scene of the exile sits right beside the next shock.

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering; confirm.
Ayodhya 94–95 come after Bharata sets out in the text; the script says so plainly and reads the scene here as the picture of the Chitrakoot days. A Keeper may prefer to keep it in Valmiki's order.
The colors of the peaks and Rama's words about not grieving for the kingdom: paraphrased; confirm.
The mountain as Ayodhya, the deer as citizens, the Mandakini as the Sarayu (Ayodhya 95): confirm.
Close screen shortens tomorrow's title to its index word ('Dasharatha's death and the curse').
Reviewer: Rama's 'two good things' (his father's word kept, Bharata's joy) replaces the earlier 'I'm here with you', which was not in the verse; confirm against Ayodhya 94.
Reviewer: the transition to Sumantra's return now says the story goes back to Valmiki's order (Ayodhya 57 precedes 94), since the scene was moved forward.
Review (538–556 pass): review question now picks up day 540's new carry; 'a week ago' (Sumitra's line is days 532–533) softened; howItsDone no longer claims what many Hindus or pilgrims remember.
